mainTopic: Returning a stolen lamb with or without the owner's knowledge, and which goods may be bought from shepherds and watchmen
overview: The amud opens by finishing the discussion of a thief who returns a stolen lamb to the flock. רבא explains that רב חסדא requires the owner's knowledge because the lamb has learned to wander and needs closer watching. The גמרא then defends רבא and רב against contradictions from their own other statements: רבא's case is one where the owner never counted, and רב's lenient case is about a spotted lamb the owner recognizes right away. Next the גמרא tries to find these arguments among the תנאים, in the ברייתא of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא, and in two ברייתות about a robber who slipped the repayment into a business payment. Each match is pushed away, partly by using רבי יצחק's rule that a person checks his purse all the time. A new משנה then teaches what may and may not be bought from shepherds, watchmen and women, and that anything the seller asks you to hide is forbidden. A ברייתא adds details, and the גמרא explains its numbers (four, five, and the problem of three sheep) with one test: would the owner notice the loss? Finally a second ברייתא shows that רבי יהודה's split between home animals and wilderness animals is a leniency.

steps.title: Why does רב חסדא require the owner's knowledge?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב חסדא's ruling that the lamb must be returned with the owner's knowledge when the owner did not know about the theft.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רב חסדא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב חסדא rules the way he does. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא said that when the owner never knew about the theft, simply counting the flock is not enough, and the owner must actually know the lamb came back. That sounds backwards at first, since the owner never knew anything was missing. So the גמרא wants the logic behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner's knowledge that the lamb was returned

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rav Ḥisda?
phrases.notes: רבא is explaining רב חסדא's ruling from just before, where the owner didn't know about the theft.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens an explanation of a ruling stated just before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The logical reason behind רב חסדא's requirement of the owner's knowledge when the owner was unaware of the theft.

steps.title: The lamb has learned to wander
steps.stepSummary: Because the thief taught the lamb to step outside its usual place, it now needs closer watching, so the owner must be told.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the thief got the lamb used to taking steps outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer: once the thief took the lamb out, the lamb has gotten into the habit of leaving the flock.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply putting the lamb back is not a full return, because the lamb is now more likely to stray again. Only an owner who knows what happened can give it the extra watching it now needs. So the owner's knowledge is part of a proper return.

keyTerms.meaning: He got it used to, he trained it
Steps outside, the habit of walking away from home

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why returning a stolen animal can mean more than putting it back physically. The owner has to be able to guard it properly.

phrases.english: Since he got it used to
phrases.notes: "He" is the thief, and "it" is the lamb.

phrases.english: steps outside.
phrases.notes: Literally "outside footsteps." The lamb has gotten into the habit of leaving the owner's property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The lamb has been trained to wander, so it needs more supervision. Only an owner who knows can provide it, so a return requires the owner's knowledge.

steps.title: Did רבא really say this? His case of the shouted-at thief
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא assumes רבא agrees with רב חסדא and challenges this from another ruling of רבא: a thief who dropped a lamb when the owner shouted is liable if the owner doesn't know whether it was returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבא really say this? But רבא said: someone who saw another person lift a lamb from his flock, shouted at him, and the thief threw it down, and the owner doesn't know if it went back or not, and then it died or was stolen, the thief is responsible for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions whether רבא really holds like רב חסדא. It quotes a different ruling of רבא that seems to point the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבא explained רב חסדא's reason, the גמרא assumes רבא agrees with him. רב חסדא holds that when the owner knew about the theft, counting the flock is enough. In רבא's case the owner saw the theft, yet the thief stays liable, and the next step shows how this creates a contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: Did he really say? (opens a challenge from the same person's other words)
He raised his voice at him, shouted at him
He threw it down, dropped it
He is responsible for it, he must pay if it is lost

phrases.english: And did Rava say this?
But didn't Rava say:
This one who saw his fellow
who lifted a lamb from his flock,
and he shouted at him, and he threw it down,
phrases.notes: The owner shouted, and the thief dropped the lamb.

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא יְדַע אִי הֲדַרָה אִי לָא הֲדַרָה,
phrases.english: and he does not know whether it returned or did not return,
and it died or was stolen –
he is liable for its responsibility.
phrases.notes: "He" is the thief. He has to pay for the lamb.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רָבָא הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption that רבא, who explained רב חסדא, agrees with his ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that רבא holds like רב חסדא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא makes the thief liable in a case where the owner knew about the theft. Under רב חסדא, counting the flock would have been enough to exempt him.

steps.title: Even if the owner counted the flock?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sharpens the challenge: presumably רבא makes the thief liable even if the owner counted the flock, which goes against רב חסדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this true even if he counted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out exactly where the contradiction is. It suggests רבא's ruling applies even when the owner counted his flock afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב חסדא, when the owner knew about the theft, a full count of the flock exempts the thief. If רבא says the thief is liable even after a count, then רבא disagrees with רב חסדא. This finishes the challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it so that...? (proposes a reading to build a challenge)

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו אַף עַל גַּב דִּמְנִי?
phrases.english: What, is it not even though he counted?
phrases.notes: "He" is the owner, counting his flock after the incident and finding it complete.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי, לָאו אַף עַל גַּב דִּמְנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge of step 3 by identifying the case that contradicts רב חסדא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If רבא's ruling holds even when the owner counted, then counting does not exempt the thief. That contradicts רב חסדא's view that counting is enough when the owner knew of the theft.

steps.title: No, the owner did not count
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבא's ruling is only about a case where the owner never counted the flock.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is a case where he did not count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge. רבא's case is one where the owner never counted the flock, so there is no contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without a count, nothing shows the owner that the lamb is back. So of course the thief stays liable. רבא can still agree with רב חסדא that a count would have been enough.
steps.whatToRemember: רבא's "shouted-at thief" ruling is about an owner who never counted. So רבא can still agree with רב חסדא that counting is enough when the owner knew about the theft.

phrases.english: No, where he did not count.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 3-4 by narrowing רבא's case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא's ruling applies even when the owner counted the flock, which would contradict רב חסדא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבא's ruling applies only when the owner did not count, so it fits with רב חסדא.

steps.title: Did רב really say this? Returning to a flock in the wilderness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב's earlier position from another statement of his: a thief who returns the lamb to the flock in the wilderness has done his duty.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רב really say this? But רב said: if he returned it to the flock that is in the wilderness, he has fulfilled his obligation!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to רב's earlier ruling. It quotes another statement of רב that seems to contradict it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רב ruled that when the owner knew about the theft, the owner must also know about the return. Here רב says simply putting the lamb back into the flock out in the wilderness is enough. That suggests the owner does not need to know about the return at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Wilderness, open grazing land away from town

phrases.english: And did Rav say this?
phrases.notes: "This" is רב's earlier ruling about returning the lamb, from before this section.

phrases.english: But didn't Rav say:
If he returned it to the flock that is in the wilderness –
he has fulfilled his obligation!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אָמַר רַב הָכִי? וְהָאָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from רבא to a challenge against רב's own earlier ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's earlier ruling that when the owner knew of the theft, the return requires the owner's knowledge.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב exempts a thief who just put the lamb back in the wilderness flock. That seems to require no knowledge and no counting, which contradicts his earlier ruling.

steps.title: רב agrees about a spotted lamb
steps.stepSummary: רב חנן בר אבא answers that רב's lenient ruling is only about a lamb with distinctive spots, which the owner recognizes right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנן בר אבא said: רב agrees in the case of a spotted lamb.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חנן בר אבא resolves the contradiction in רב's words. Putting the lamb back is enough only when the lamb is spotted and easy to recognize.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A spotted lamb stands out, so the owner notices right away that it is back. That works like the owner's knowledge. So רב still holds that the owner must know, and in this case he knows automatically.

keyTerms.meaning: A spotted (patched) animal that is easy to recognize

steps.whatToRemember: רב's two statements fit together. Normally a return needs the owner's knowledge, but a spotted lamb is recognized right away, so returning it to the flock is enough.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that what matters is whether the owner actually becomes aware the animal is back. Telling him, counting, or a recognizable animal can each do that.

phrases.english: Rav Ḥanan bar Abba said:
Rav concedes in the case of a spotted one.
phrases.notes: A spotted lamb stands out, so the owner notices right away that it's back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָנָן בַּר אַבָּא: מוֹדֶה רַב בִּרְקוֹעָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by limiting רב's lenient ruling to a recognizable lamb.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to a special exception
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב exempts any thief who returns the lamb to the wilderness flock, even without the owner's knowledge.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב exempts him only for a spotted lamb, whose return the owner notices right away. That counts as the owner's knowledge.

steps.title: Maybe this is an older dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the argument about returning a stolen item may go back to a ברייתא: רבי ישמעאל says return it to its place, and רבי עקיבא says the owner must know.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is like a dispute of תנאים: one who steals a lamb from a flock or a סלע from a purse must return it to the place he stole it from. These are the words of רבי ישמעאל. רבי עקיבא says: the owner must know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a comparison. It brings a ברייתא to see if our אמוראים are just repeating an older argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל says putting the item back where it was is enough. רבי עקיבא says the owner has to know it was returned. The next step will try to match these two views to the אמוראים we already saw.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it is like a dispute of תנאים

phrases.english: Let us say it is like a dispute of tannaim:
One who steals a lamb from the flock,
or a sela coin from the purse,
should return it to the place he stole it from;
these are the words of Rabbi Yishmael.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: צָרִיךְ דַּעַת בְּעָלִים.
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says: the owner's knowledge is required.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבא and רב, the גמרא now looks for an older source behind the disputes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do the אמוראים disputes about returning a stolen item match the ברייתא's dispute between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא?

steps.title: First try: it matches רב and שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The Sages assumed that everyone accepts רבי יצחק's rule that a person checks his purse all the time, so the stolen סלע is a case where the owner knew. So maybe the ברייתא matches the dispute of רב and שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They assumed everyone holds like רבי יצחק, who said a person tends to feel his purse all the time. So isn't the ברייתא about a סלע whose theft the owner knew about, and the same as the dispute of רב and שמואל?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes its first guess about which earlier dispute the ברייתא matches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since people feel their purse all the time, the owner of the סלע will soon notice it is gone. So this is a theft the owner knew about. That is the case רב and שמואל argued about, so maybe רב agrees with רבי עקיבא and שמואל with רבי ישמעאל.

keyTerms.meaning: To feel or check his purse
What, is it not...? (introduces a suggested reading)

phrases.english: They assumed that everyone
holds the view of Rabbi Yitzchak,
as Rabbi Yitzchak said:

phrases.aramaic: אָדָם עָשׂוּי לְמַשְׁמֵשׁ בְּכִיסוֹ בְּכׇל שָׁעָה.
phrases.english: A person tends to feel his purse all the time.
phrases.notes: So the owner quickly notices the coin is missing, and the theft counts as one he knew about.

phrases.english: What, is it not about a sela stolen with the owner's knowledge,
and the same as the dispute of Rav and Shmuel?

steps.triggerLanguage: סַבְרוּהָ, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a specific match for the ברייתא brought in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the ברייתא about a theft the owner knew about, matching רב and שמואל?

steps.title: No, it matches רב חסדא and רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the first match. The ברייתא's argument is about the lamb, stolen without the owner knowing, so it matches רב חסדא and רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is about a lamb stolen without the owner knowing, and it matches the dispute of רב חסדא and רבי יוחנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the first guess and offers a different match.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of the argument is the lamb, not the סלע. A lamb can be taken without the owner noticing. That is the case רב חסדא and רבי יוחנן argued about, so רב חסדא would agree with רבי עקיבא and רבי יוחנן with רבי ישמעאל.

phrases.english: No; it is about a lamb stolen without the owner's knowledge,
and the same as the dispute of Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 9's match and replaces it with another.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the link to רב and שמואל, not the idea that the ברייתא matches some אמוראים dispute.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא's argument is about the lamb, stolen without the owner knowing, not about the סלע.

steps.title: רב זביד: the argument is about a שומר who stole
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא says everyone agrees with רב חסדא when a שומר stole from the owner's area. The תנאים only argue when a שומר stole from his own area: did his guarding job end when he stole?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: when a שומר stole from the owner's area, everyone agrees with רב חסדא. They argue only when a שומר stole from his own area, whether he may return it to where he took it. רבי עקיבא holds his guarding ended. רבי ישמעאל holds his guarding did not end.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד gives a new explanation of the ברייתא. It is not about the אמוראים disputes at all, but about a שומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a שומר takes from the owner's area, everyone agrees the owner must know it was returned, like רב חסדא. If he takes from his own area, the question is whether stealing ended his job as guard. If it ended (רבי עקיבא), he must tell the owner. If it did not end (רבי ישמעאל), putting it back in his own area is enough, since he is still guarding it.

keyTerms.meaning: A person paid or trusted to guard someone else's property

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב זביד, everyone agrees with רב חסדא in the normal case. The ברייתא only argues about a שומר who stole from his own area: does stealing end his job as guard?
steps.confusionAlert: Here the thief is the שומר himself, not a stranger. So 'returning to the place he stole from' means putting it back in his own area.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava:
With a guardian who stole from the owner's area,

phrases.aramaic: כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי, כִּדְרַב חִסְדָּא;
phrases.english: everyone agrees, like Rav Chisda;
and here it is about a guardian who stole from his own area,
whether he may return it to the place he stole from, that they argue.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא סָבַר: כָּלְתָה לוֹ שְׁמִירָתוֹ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva holds: his guarding has ended,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל סָבַר: לֹא כָּלְתָה לוֹ שְׁמִירָתוֹ.
phrases.english: and Rabbi Yishmael holds: his guarding has not ended.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the ברייתא, so it no longer has to match any of the אמוראים disputes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a שומר stole from the owner's area, all agree the owner must know of the return, like רב חסדא. When a שומר stole from his own area, רבי עקיבא says his guarding ended so the owner must know. רבי ישמעאל says his guarding did not end, so returning it to his own area is enough.

steps.title: Is the counting question an old argument between תנאים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the argument over whether counting exempts the thief goes back to two ברייתות about a robber who hid the repayment inside a business payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that 'counting exempts' is an argument of תנאים? It was taught: someone who robbed his friend and then slipped the repayment into a business payment. One ברייתא says he has done his duty, and another says he has not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a pair of ברייתות that seem to argue. It suggests they may be the source for the question of whether counting exempts the thief.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The robber paid back secretly by adding the stolen amount to a different payment, so the owner never heard the words 'this is what I stole.' One ברייתא says that is enough, and the other says it is not. The גמרא wonders whether this is the same question as a lamb returned to the flock that the owner later counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Counting exempts: if the owner counts his things and finds them all there, the thief is free.
It is an argument between תנאים, the Sages of the משנה period.
He slipped it into the bill, hiding the repayment inside another payment.
He has done his duty / he has not done his duty.

phrases.english: Shall we say that 'counting exempts' is an argument of תנאים?
phrases.notes: 'Counting' means the owner counts his things, sees nothing is missing, and so the thief is off the hook.

phrases.english: As it was taught: one who robs his friend
and slipped it to him inside a bill
phrases.notes: He paid the owner extra in some other deal, so the stolen money came back without the owner being told.

phrases.english: One ברייתא teaches: he has done his duty,
and another ברייתא teaches: he has not done his duty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After trying to match the lamb dispute to the ברייתא of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא (which רב זביד then explained differently), the גמרא now tests whether the 'counting' question has a source among the תנאים.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the question of whether counting exempts the thief the same as the argument between these two ברייתות?

steps.title: Assuming everyone accepts רבי יצחק, the ברייתות seem to argue about counting
steps.stepSummary: The Sages assume both ברייתות accept רבי יצחק's rule that a person checks his purse all the time. If so, the only thing left to argue about is whether counting exempts the thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: They assumed everyone accepts רבי יצחק, who said a person usually feels his purse all the time. So isn't this what they argue about? The one who says 'he has done his duty' holds that counting exempts, and the one who says 'he has not' holds that counting does not exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the two ברייתות must be arguing about counting. Since the owner will surely check his purse and count his money, the only open question is whether that counting is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because of רבי יצחק, the owner will soon count his coins and find the full amount there. He still does not know it was a repayment for the robbery. So the ברייתא that frees the robber must hold that counting exempts, and the other ברייתא must hold it does not.

keyTerms.meaning: They assumed (the Sages who were discussing the question).
A person usually feels and checks his purse.
Isn't it this point that they argue about?

phrases.english: They assumed that everyone
accepts the rule of רבי יצחק,
who said: a person usually feels his purse
every single hour.
phrases.notes: So the owner will soon notice and count the money he received.

phrases.english: Isn't it about this that they argue?

phrases.aramaic: דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר יָצָא, סָבַר: מִנְיָן פּוֹטֵר;
phrases.english: The one who says he has done his duty holds that counting exempts;

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאן דְּאָמַר לֹא יָצָא, סָבַר: מִנְיָן אֵינוֹ פּוֹטֵר?
phrases.english: and the one who says he has not done his duty holds that counting does not exempt?

steps.triggerLanguage: סַבְרוּהָ, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the reasoning behind the suggestion in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: If both ברייתות accept רבי יצחק, isn't their argument just about whether counting exempts?

steps.title: No, they argue about whether רבי יצחק's rule is true
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: if רבי יצחק is right, everyone would agree that counting exempts. So the ברייתות really argue about רבי יצחק's rule itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: if we accept רבי יצחק, everyone agrees counting exempts. Rather, they argue about רבי יצחק's rule: one Sage accepts it and one does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the idea that the ברייתות argue about counting. It says they argue about whether a person really checks his purse all the time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the owner checks his purse and counts the money, everyone agrees the robber is free. The ברייתא that says 'he has not done his duty' simply does not believe the owner will check and count. So the ברייתות tell us nothing about the counting question.

keyTerms.term: מָר אִית לֵיהּ / וּמָר לֵית לֵיהּ
keyTerms.meaning: One Sage accepts it / and the other Sage does not accept it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי: אִי סְבִירָא לַן כְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק –
phrases.english: They answered: if we hold like רבי יצחק,

phrases.aramaic: כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּמִנְיָן פּוֹטֵר;
phrases.english: everyone agrees that counting exempts;
rather, they argue about רבי יצחק's rule:
one Sage accepts רבי יצחק's rule,
and the other Sage does not accept רבי יצחק's rule.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: אִי סְבִירָא לַן כְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the assumption in step 13 that both ברייתות accept רבי יצחק.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the 'counting' question is an argument between תנאים.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed both ברייתות accept רבי יצחק. In fact, the argument may be about רבי יצחק's rule itself.

steps.title: Or: everyone accepts רבי יצחק, and the ברייתות discuss different cases
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: both ברייתות accept רבי יצחק. One is talking about money put into the owner's purse, and the other about money put into his hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say that everyone accepts רבי יצחק, and there is no contradiction. This ברייתא is where he counted the money and put it into the owner's purse, and that ברייתא is where he counted it and put it into his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second way to push off the proof. The two ברייתות do not argue at all; they are describing two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Money put straight into the purse will be found when the owner checks it, so the robber has done his duty. Money handed to the owner may be mixed with his other coins and never noticed, so the robber has not done his duty. Either way, the ברייתות give no source for the counting question.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: this brings a second, different answer.
And there is no contradiction between the two sources.
He counted the money and put it in.

steps.whatToRemember: The try to find 'counting exempts' as an argument between תנאים does not work. The two ברייתות can be explained as an argument about רבי יצחק's purse-checking rule, or as two different cases: purse or hand.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק;
phrases.english: everyone accepts רבי יצחק's rule;
and there is no contradiction:
this one is where he counted it and put it into his purse,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא that says 'he has done his duty'; the owner will find the money when he checks his purse.

phrases.english: and that one is where he counted it and put it into his hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second way to reject the proof, this time keeping the assumption that everyone accepts רבי יצחק.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the two ברייתות, even if both accept רבי יצחק.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתות may be talking about two different cases (purse or hand), not two opinions about counting.

steps.title: A third answer: it depends on whether there was other money in the purse
steps.stepSummary: Both ברייתות talk about money that was counted and placed in the owner's purse. One means the owner already had other money there, and the other means he did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: both ברייתות talk about a robber who counted the money and put it in the owner's purse. One ברייתא means the owner had other coins in his purse. The other means he had no other coins in his purse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to explain why the two ברייתות disagree, without saying they argue about the הלכה at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner had no other coins, he will notice the extra money when he counts, so he knows he was repaid. If he already had other coins and did not know how many, he cannot notice the extra amount, so the repayment does not count. Like Step 15, this keeps both ברייתות in line with רבי יצחק and just splits the cases.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces another possible answer
Both this one and that one: both sources are talking about the same basic case

steps.whatToRemember: The second and third answers both say the ברייתות agree with רבי יצחק. They differ in the details: hand versus purse, or a purse with other money versus an empty purse.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
both this one and that one
are where he counted it and put it in his purse;
phrases.notes: 'He' is the robber, and 'his purse' is the owner's purse.

phrases.english: this one is where he has
other coins in his purse,
phrases.notes: With other coins already there, the owner can't notice the extra money when he counts, so he doesn't know he was paid back.

phrases.english: that one is where he does not have
other coins in his purse.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי דִּמְנִי וּרְמָא בְּכִיסֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternative to Step 15's split between hand and purse. This answer splits between a purse that had other money in it and one that did not.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the ברייתות argue about whether counting exempts the robber.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתות can be describing two different cases, with or without other coins in the purse, so they do not have to disagree about the law.

steps.title: New משנה: items one may not buy from shepherds and watchmen
steps.stepSummary: The משנה forbids buying wool, milk and young goats from shepherds, and wood and produce from produce watchmen.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may not buy wool, milk or young goats from shepherds. One may not buy wood or produce from people who guard produce.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists items one may not buy from people who look after someone else's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Shepherds and watchmen take care of things that belong to other people. The items listed are exactly what they guard, so there is a real worry they are selling the owner's property without permission. Buying from them would help a thief.

keyTerms.meaning: Shepherds who tend other people's flocks
Watchmen who guard someone else's produce

phrases.english: MISHNA: One may not buy from shepherds
wool, milk, or young goats,
and not from produce watchmen
wood or produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not buy from shepherds or produce watchmen the items they are in charge of guarding, because those items may be stolen.

steps.title: What may be bought from women, the hiding rule, and eggs and chickens
steps.stepSummary: One may buy certain goods from women in certain regions. Anything the seller asks you to hide is forbidden. Eggs and chickens may be bought anywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: But one may buy woolen goods from women in יהודה, linen goods in the גליל, and calves in the שרון. For all of these, if the seller asked the buyer to hide the purchase, it is forbidden. One may buy eggs and chickens anywhere.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with cases where buying is allowed. Then it adds a warning sign that makes even those purchases forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In these regions women commonly work with these goods, so we assume they are selling with the owner's permission. If the seller says to keep it hidden, that is a strong sign the item is stolen, so it becomes forbidden. Eggs and chickens are allowed everywhere.
steps.confusionAlert: 'All of them' that the seller asks to hide includes even the items the משנה just allowed. Being permitted in general does not help once the seller asks for secrecy.

phrases.english: But one may buy from women
woolen goods in Judea,
and linen goods in the Galilee,
and calves in the Sharon.
And all of these, where they said to hide it, are forbidden.
phrases.notes: 'They' are the sellers, telling the buyer to keep the purchase hidden.

phrases.english: And one may buy eggs and chickens from anywhere.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה. After the forbidden cases, it lists permitted ones and a limit on them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Buying is allowed where the seller is presumed to have permission. A request to hide the purchase makes it forbidden. Eggs and chickens may always be bought.

steps.title: A ברייתא adds detail about buying from shepherds
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא forbids buying goats, kids, fleeces or loose wool from shepherds. It allows sewn garments, and allows milk and cheese in the wilderness but not in a settled area.
steps.simpleTranslation: תנו רבנן: One may not buy from shepherds goats, kids, fleeces or torn pieces of wool. But one may buy sewn garments from them, because those belong to them. And one may buy milk and cheese from them in the wilderness, but not in a settled area.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by quoting a ברייתא that expands on the משנה's rule about shepherds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא adds whole animals and raw wool to the forbidden list. It also adds two permissions the משנה did not mention. Sewn garments are presumed to be the shepherd's own. Milk and cheese may be bought in the wilderness but not in a settled area.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
One may not buy from shepherds
not goats and not kids

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא גִּיזִּין וְלֹא תְּלוּשִׁין שֶׁל צֶמֶר,
phrases.english: and not fleeces and not torn pieces of wool,
but one may buy sewn items from them,
because they are theirs.
And one may buy milk and cheese from them
in the wilderness, but not in a settled area.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין לוֹקְחִין מִן הָרוֹעִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the משנה's rule about shepherds from Step 17 with more items and new permissions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Animals and raw wool may not be bought from shepherds. Sewn garments may be bought. Milk and cheese may be bought in the wilderness but not in a settled area.

steps.title: Four or five sheep may be bought, but not two
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: one may buy four or five sheep or fleeces from a shepherd, but not two.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one may buy from them four or five sheep, or four or five fleeces. But one may not buy two sheep, and not two fleeces.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the last step keeps going. It says a larger amount, four or five, may be bought from a shepherd, but a small amount like two may not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shepherd would not risk stealing a big group of animals, because the owner would notice. Two missing animals are easy to hide, so a sale of two looks like theft.
steps.confusionAlert: It sounds backwards, but buying MORE is allowed and buying LESS is forbidden. A large sale is less likely to be stolen goods, because the owner would notice that much missing.

phrases.english: And one may buy from them
four or five sheep,
four or five fleeces;
but not two sheep
and not two fleeces.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continuation of the same ברייתא quoted in step 19
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Four or five sheep or fleeces may be bought from a shepherd, but not two.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's view and the general rule: would the owner notice?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה allows buying animals kept at home but not wilderness animals. The ברייתא's general rule is that if the owner would notice the item missing, one may buy it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: animals kept at home may be bought from them, but wilderness animals may not be bought from them. The general rule: anything the shepherd sells that the owner would notice may be bought from them. If the owner would not notice it, it may not be bought from them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה adds a distinction between animals kept at home and animals kept in the wilderness. Then the ברייתא sums up everything with one general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animals that come home are checked by the owner, so a missing one would be noticed and the shepherd would not dare steal it. Wilderness animals are rarely checked, so they are easier to steal. The general rule ties all the cases together: what matters is whether the owner would notice.

keyTerms.meaning: Animals kept out in the wilderness
The general rule of the matter

steps.whatToRemember: The key test for buying from a shepherd: would the owner notice the item missing? If yes, you may buy. If no, you may not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This general rule explains all the earlier details, like four or five versus two, and home animals versus wilderness animals.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
animals kept at home, one may buy from them;
wilderness animals, one may not buy from them.
The general rule of the matter:
anything that the shepherd sells
and the owner would notice it
one may buy from them;
if he would not notice it
one may not buy from them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בַּיָּיתוֹת לוֹקְחִין מֵהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the ברייתא with רבי יהודה's distinction and a summary rule
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Buying is allowed when the owner would notice the item missing, and forbidden when he would not.

steps.title: If four is allowed, why mention five?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if buying four is already allowed, then five is obviously allowed too, so why does the ברייתא say 'five'?
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: one may buy from them four or five sheep, four or five fleeces. Now, if you can say we may buy four, is it even necessary to say five?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the opening line of the ברייתא and questions its wording. Saying 'five' seems to add nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning is that a bigger number is less likely to be stolen. So if four is allowed, five should be allowed even more. Mentioning five looks extra, and the גמרא expects every word to teach something.

phrases.english: The Master said:
one may buy from them four or five sheep,
four or five fleeces.
Now that it can be said
we buy four,
is five even needed?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא יֵשׁ לוֹמַר אַרְבַּע זָבְנִינַן, חָמֵשׁ מִיבַּעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Examines the wording of the ברייתא just quoted
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'four or five' in the ברייתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the smaller number, four, is allowed, the larger number, five, is obviously allowed, so mentioning five is extra.

steps.title: רב חסדא: four out of a flock of five
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא explains that the ברייתא means buying four sheep from a flock that has only five.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: it means four out of five.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the question. The numbers are not two separate options; 'five' is the size of the flock.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is teaching that you may buy four sheep even from a flock of only five. A shepherd would not dare steal four out of five, since the owner would surely notice. So 'five' is not extra; it describes the flock.

keyTerms.meaning: Four out of (a flock of) five

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
four out of five.
phrases.notes: He means buying four sheep from a flock that only has five in total.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: אַרְבַּע מִתּוֹךְ חָמֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the extra word 'five'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the numbers: 'five' is the flock size, not a second amount
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Four and five are two possible amounts to buy, so 'five' is extra.
steps.terutzMaskana: One may buy four sheep from a flock of only five.

steps.title: Another version: four from a small flock, five from a large one
steps.stepSummary: Another version of רב חסדא's answer: four may be bought from a small flock, and five from a large flock.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say רב חסדא said: four from a small flock, and five from a large flock.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of what רב חסדא said. Here the two numbers match two different flock sizes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a small flock, four is already big enough that the owner would notice. With a large flock, you need five before the owner would notice. So 'five' is not extra; it is the minimum for a large flock.

phrases.english: And some say:
Rav Chisda said:
four from a small flock,
and five from a large flock.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second version of רב חסדא's answer to the same question
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each number fits a different flock size
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Five' adds nothing once four is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Four is enough for a small flock; a large flock needs five.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself about three sheep
steps.stepSummary: The opening of the ברייתא implies three sheep may not be bought, but the ending implies three may be bought.
steps.simpleTranslation: This itself is difficult. You said: four or five sheep, four or five fleeces. That means four or five, yes, but three, no. Now say the end: but not two sheep. That implies we may buy three!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction inside the ברייתא itself. Each half hints at an opposite ruling about three sheep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening says the minimum is four, so three should be forbidden. The ending only forbids two, which hints that three is allowed. Both hints cannot be correct, so the גמרא needs to explain the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: This statement itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)
Say (look at) the end of the text

steps.confusionAlert: No one actually says 'three' here. Both rulings about three are only inferred, one from each half of the ברייתא, and that is why they clash.

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
you said:
"four or five sheep,
four or five fleeces,"
four or five, yes,
but three, no;
say the end part:
"but not two sheep"
which implies we may buy three!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new difficulty on the same ברייתא line, separate from the 'five' question
steps.kashyaTarget: The opening and closing clauses of the ברייתא in step 20
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The opening implies three is forbidden (minimum four), while the ending implies three is allowed (only two is forbidden).

steps.title: Healthy sheep versus weak sheep
steps.stepSummary: The contradiction about three sheep is settled. Three may be bought when the sheep are strong, but not when they are weak.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. One part of the ברייתא is talking about strong, healthy sheep, and the other part is talking about weak, frail sheep.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 25 by saying that each part of the ברייתא is talking about a different kind of sheep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner watches his strong sheep closely, so he would notice if even three went missing, and buying three is allowed. He cares less about weak sheep, so three might go missing without him noticing, and buying three is not allowed. The test is still the same one from step 21: would the owner notice?

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. The question has an answer.

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
this one is about strong, healthy sheep,
phrases.notes: Don't mix this word up with 'ברייתא', the teaching. Here it means healthy, well-fed animals.

phrases.english: and that one is about weak, frail sheep.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 25
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases: each part of the ברייתא is talking about a different condition of the animals
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both parts of the ברייתא seemed to be talking about the same three sheep and to give opposite rulings.
steps.terutzMaskana: Buying three strong sheep is allowed, because the owner would notice them missing. Buying three weak sheep is not allowed, because he might not notice.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the number of animals is not a fixed rule. What decides it is whether the owner would actually notice the loss.

steps.title: Which part of the ברייתא is רבי יהודה reacting to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה again and asks: is he adding a stricter rule to the opening of the ברייתא, or a more lenient rule to its ending?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: you may buy home animals from them, but not wilderness animals. The question was asked: is רבי יהודה reacting to the opening of the ברייתא, which would make his rule stricter? Or is he reacting to the ending, which would make his rule more lenient?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back רבי יהודה's words (from step 21) and asks a real question about them. This sets up a longer explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening of the ברייתא allows buying four or five sheep. The ending forbids buying two. רבי יהודה's split between home animals and wilderness animals could be attached to either rule, and the result would be very different in each case.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before the חכמים, a real open question
The opening part of a ברייתא or משנה
The ending part of a ברייתא or משנה
He is standing on, meaning he is referring to

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
home animals, one may buy from them,
wilderness animals, one may not buy from them, etc.
A question was asked before them:
Is Rabbi Yehuda referring to the opening clause, to be stricter;
or maybe he is referring to the ending clause, to be more lenient?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling the contradiction about three sheep (steps 25-26), the גמרא returns to רבי יהודה's words in the ברייתא and opens a new question about them
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is רבי יהודה's split between home animals and wilderness animals attached to the opening rule (four or five allowed) or to the ending rule (two forbidden)?

steps.title: Spelling out both sides of the question
steps.stepSummary: Stricter reading: wilderness animals may not be bought, even four or five. More lenient reading: home animals may be bought, even two.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is referring to the opening and being stricter, he means this: 'You may buy four or five sheep' applies only to home animals, but wilderness animals may not be bought even four or five at a time. Or maybe he is referring to the ending and being more lenient, meaning this: 'But not two sheep and not two fleeces' applies only to wilderness animals, but home animals may be bought even two at a time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains exactly what each side of the question would mean in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the strict reading, רבי יהודה takes away part of the permission in the opening, so wilderness flocks are completely off-limits. On the lenient reading, he takes away part of the ban in the ending, so home animals may be bought even in a small number like two. Each reading changes a different number in the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Home animals, kept near the house
Wilderness animals, grazing far out in the fields

phrases.english: Is he referring to the opening, to be stricter,
since it said: 'One may buy four or five sheep from them,'
that applies only to home animals,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מִדְבָּרִיּוֹת – אֲפִילּוּ אַרְבַּע וְחָמֵשׁ לֹא;
phrases.english: but wilderness animals, not even four or five;
or maybe he is referring to the ending, to be more lenient,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: ״אֲבָל לֹא שְׁתֵּי צֹאן וְלֹא שְׁתֵּי גִיזִּין״,
phrases.english: since it said: 'But not two sheep and not two fleeces,'
that applies only to wilderness animals,
but home animals, one may buy even two?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the two sides of the question asked in step 27
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which practical result does רבי יהודה mean: a full ban on wilderness animals, or permission to buy even two home animals?
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה's words are the same in both readings. What changes is which rule in the ברייתא he is adjusting, and so whether his words make things stricter or more lenient.

steps.title: Four or five may always be bought, so רבי יהודה is being lenient
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי יהודה saying that four or five sheep may be bought anywhere. So he is not making the opening stricter; he is making the ending more lenient.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as a ברייתא teaches: רבי יהודה says, you may buy home animals from them, and you may not buy wilderness animals from them. And everywhere, you may buy four or five sheep from them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that answers the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא says that 'everywhere,' for both home animals and wilderness animals, four or five sheep may be bought. So רבי יהודה does not forbid buying four or five wilderness animals, and the strict reading falls away. What remains is the lenient reading: his split is about the small number, and he allows buying even two home animals.

keyTerms.meaning: Everywhere, meaning in every case, home or wilderness

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יהודה, four or five sheep may always be bought. His split is only about small numbers: two home animals may be bought, but two wilderness animals may not.

phrases.english: Come and hear, as it is taught in a ברייתא:
Rabbi Yehuda says:
One may buy home animals from them,
and one may not buy wilderness animals from them.

phrases.aramaic: וּבְכׇל מָקוֹם לוֹקְחִין מֵהֶן אַרְבַּע וְחָמֵשׁ צֹאן.
phrases.english: And everywhere, one may buy four or five sheep from them.
phrases.notes: 'Everywhere' is the key word. Even wilderness animals may be bought four or five at a time, so רבי יהודה isn't being stricter on the opening.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from steps 27 and 28 using an outside ברייתא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה is referring to the ending and is being lenient: four or five may be bought everywhere, and home animals may be bought even two at a time.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that quotes רבי יהודה with the added words 'and everywhere, one may buy four or five sheep'
